common_name: Corky Daylily (Classic Miniature Bronze-Backed Yellow Spider Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained soil in full sun; Corky is a classic small-flowered diploid daylily prized for its wiry, branched scapes held well above narrow, grass-like foliage.

directions: Corky bears small, trumpet-shaped, bright golden-yellow flowers with a bronze-maroon reverse and buds, carried in profusion on tall, thin, well-branched scapes that stand high above slender, grassy foliage, giving the whole plant a wildflower-like habit rather than the bold look of modern hybrids. Long grown as a garden and breeding standard, it earned an American Hemerocallis Society Honorable Mention in 1963 and the Donn Fischer Memorial Cup in 1967. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain its heavy, long-lasting bloom display.

common_name: Siloam Paul Watts Daylily (Velvety Red Siloam Series Miniature Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in moist, fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; one of Pauline Henry's celebrated Siloam-series small-flowered daylilies bred in Siloam Springs, Arkansas.

directions: Registered by Pauline Henry in 1988, Siloam Paul Watts produces velvety, deep red, ruffled flowers with a green-yellow throat on a compact, floriferous diploid plant, and it went on to receive American Hemerocallis Society awards in the 1990s. Like other members of Henry's influential Siloam series, it combines heavy substance and round form on a garden-worthy, easy-care plant. Divide crowded clumps every three to four years in spring to keep flowering vigorous.

common_name: Red Hot Returns Daylily (Everblooming Cherry-Red Reblooming Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; a patented (US Plant Patent PP13,499), heavily reblooming diploid bred by Darrel Apps as part of his 'Returns' series of near-continuous-flowering daylilies.

directions: Bred by Darrel Apps and patented in 2003, Red Hot Returns bears bright cherry-red flowers on a compact plant that blooms nearly continuously for up to 100 days in a typical growing season, forming multiple scapes per fan rather than the single scape typical of most daylilies. It was introduced to give gardeners a true red counterpart to the earlier yellow Happy Returns and gold Stella d'Oro rebloomers. Deadhead spent scapes and divide clumps every few years to sustain its exceptionally long bloom season.

common_name: Romantic Returns Daylily (Everblooming Magenta Reblooming Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; a patented (US Plant Patent PP13,481), heavily reblooming diploid bred by Darrel Apps as part of his 'Returns' series.

directions: Bred by Darrel Apps, Romantic Returns was one of the first large-flowered, continuously reblooming daylilies in a clear, rich magenta-pink, filling a color gap left by the earlier yellow-toned Happy Returns and Stella d'Oro. It later served as the female parent of Dynamite Returns. Plants form multiple scapes per fan and flower over an extended season from late spring into fall; divide every few years to keep clumps vigorous.

common_name: Dynamite Returns Daylily (Everblooming Ruffled Rosy-Pink Reblooming Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; a patented (US Plant Patent PP20,002) reblooming diploid bred by Darrel Apps from a cross of Romantic Returns and Red Hot Returns.

directions: Bred from a 1998 cross of Romantic Returns and Red Hot Returns and patented in 2009, Dynamite Returns bears ruffled, bright rosy-pink flowers of substantial texture on a floriferous plant capable of blooming for up to 90 days per season. Like other members of Apps's Returns breeding line, it produces multiple scapes per fan with more than 30 buds per scape, giving an exceptionally long and heavy floral display. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring.

common_name: Blazing Returns Daylily (Everblooming Ruffled Red Reblooming Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; a patented (US Plant Patent PP28,560) reblooming diploid bred by Darrel Apps from a cross of Endless Heart and Regency Dandy.

directions: Patented in 2017, Blazing Returns produces ruffled red flowers with substantial texture that bloom nearly continuously for up to 75 days per season, from late June through mid-September in typical climates. Bred by Darrel Apps as part of his long-blooming Returns line, it was noted at introduction as among the first long, continuously blooming red daylilies with such heavy flower substance. Divide clumps every few years in spring to sustain vigorous rebloom.

common_name: Just Plum Happy Daylily (Everblooming Flesh-Pink Purple-Eyed Reblooming Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; a patented (US Plant Patent PP14,841) reblooming diploid bred by Darrel Apps from a cross of Strawberry Candy and Heady Wine.

directions: Bred from a 1995 cross of Strawberry Candy and Heady Wine and patented in 2004, Just Plum Happy bears bright flesh-pink flowers with a dark purple eye and a picotee edge, flowering nearly continuously for up to 90 days per season. Like other daylilies in Darrel Apps's extended-bloom breeding program, it readily produces multiple scapes per fan across the season rather than a single flush. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to maintain heavy rebloom.

common_name: Mean Mister Mustard Daylily (Everblooming Ruffled Deep Yellow Burgundy-Eyed Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, fertile soil in full sun; a patented (US Plant Patent PP20,048) reblooming diploid bred by Darrel Apps from a cross of Strawberry Candy and Barbara Keen Strout.

directions: Bred from a 1996 cross and patented in 2009, Mean Mister Mustard bears highly ruffled deep-yellow flowers accented with burgundy around the eye zone and edges, blooming nearly continuously for up to 75 days per season. It is part of Darrel Apps's long line of extended-bloom daylily introductions bred for landscape performance rather than show-bench size alone. Divide congested clumps every few years in spring to keep the plant flowering heavily.

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; a wild species native to Korea, Japan, and China.

directions: Described by Takenoshin Nakai in 1932, Hemerocallis coreana is a true wild species native to southeastern and central Korea, southern Japan, and parts of China, closely related to H. middendorffii and H. thunbergii within the East Asian daylily species complex. It bears fragrant, orange-yellow flowers on modest scapes above clumping, grass-like foliage and has been used in botanical and taxonomic studies of Korean Hemerocallis. Grow it as a species collector's plant in well-drained garden soil, dividing clumps every few years in spring to maintain vigor.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)

common_name: Nikko Daylily (Esculenta Variety of Amur Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in well-drained, moderately fertile soil in full sun to light shade; a vigorous Japanese botanical variety of Hemerocallis middendorffii known locally as nikko kisuge or zenteika.

directions: Native to Japan, Hemerocallis middendorffii var. esculenta is a robust, clump-forming botanical variety of the Amur daylily, long known in Japan as nikko kisuge or zenteika and historically valued there for its edible flower buds and blossoms, reflected in the varietal epithet esculenta (edible). It bears clusters of fragrant, orange-yellow flowers held above sturdy foliage in late spring to early summer, slightly later than the typical species. Grow it as a hardy species-type garden plant in well-drained soil, dividing clumps every few years in spring to sustain vigorous bloom.

common_name: Narrow-Leaf Tawny Daylily (Angustifolia Variety Orange Daylily)

planting.note: Plant divisions in spring in average to fertile, well-drained soil in full sun to light shade; distinguished from typical Hemerocallis fulva chiefly by narrower, more grass-like foliage.

directions: Described by John Gilbert Baker, Hemerocallis fulva var. angustifolia is an accepted botanical variety of the tawny or ditch-lily daylily, native across China, Korea, and Japan, and differs from the typical variety mainly in its narrower, more linear leaves. It produces the same tawny-orange, sterile-triploid-type flowers typical of H. fulva, spreading readily by rhizomes to naturalize in rough or roadside conditions. Best used in naturalized plantings rather than refined borders given its vigorous spreading habit; divide as needed to control spread.
sources: Plants of the World Online (Kew Science)
